There will be a lot more conversation about the homonymy of 17A.

But more importantly, Tina Fey and Amy Poehler are ALUMNAE, not ALUMNI, of SNL.  At least, last I looked, but even if there's a dictionary that allows the latter, why not include at least one male star in 50 years to make the clue above reproach?

I watch a lot of tennis and have never heard a serve-bot referred to as an ACER. I don't think I've even heard ACER used as a noun in that manner. Google agrees with me as well.

I'll also take it one step further and say that the defining quality of a serve-bot is not a good serve but a bad return game. (The preferred definition is holds more than 90% of the time and breaks less than 10% of the time.) A player like Sinner who holds 90% of the time and breaks over 30% of the time would not be a serve-bot, regardless of how good his serve is.

Yesterday's big kerfuffle was that crocheting wasn't needlecraft.  Short answer:  It does use a hook, not a needle like knitting does, but some sources do call it a "hooked needle," and many sources count in among the varieties of needlecraft.  So while it's blatantly true that it's a hook, not a knitting needle, the door is open for the clue to pass muster.

Today's to-do will be even bigger, based on the number of comments within the first 20 minutes, and I will give it a name:  ALUMNIGATE.

I was second to point this out, by less than a minute.  (I might have been first if my wife hadn't been talking in my ear about, of all things, tomorrow night's dinner, while I was writing.)

But my second comment was that despite my own misgivings (and the nagging feeling that ALUMNI was just plain wrong here), there was dictionary evidence that the masculine plural word is now acceptable as a blanket plural form.  I don't like this, but it opens the doors for the clue/answer combo to pass muster.

Again, I don't like it, but...

Maybe some of those crotchety crocheters should come to the same conclusion about the clue/answer in the Monday puzzle.
Anyone else try CAT as "battery for a mouse?"

For what it's worth, I found one source that validates the use of alumnus/alumni in the feminine. The vast majority of other sources disagree https://www.rochester.edu/communications/alumni-alumna-alumnus/

I’ll allow the AAA battery for a computer mouse, they must exist although virtually every mouse I’ve seen has AA.
However, my first thought was the about those highly annoying Zhu zhu pets, which, though being described as hamsters, are certainly mouse adjacent and do use AAAs.

I just stopped by to see if people were up in arms about the Latin word endings. I'll toss in that people very often mispronounce them as well: alumni really ought to rhyme with free, and alumnae with fry, but I usually hear them the other way around.

Some theatres, like Chicago's Steppenwolf, use the term "actor" to describe a performer of any gender, rather than using the feminine-specific term "actress." Maybe that's in the same vein as using "alumni" regardless of whether any males are involved?

25D [Tina Fey and Amy Poehler vis-à-vis "Saturday Night Live"]

Technically, when you talk about a group of more than one female graduates, you should say "ALUMNAE."

But in common usage, ALUMNI is probably prevalent.

I’m old, so I remember when "he" was the “correct” default for any unknown person, e.g.  “If a professor is ill, he should find a substitute lecturer." Most of us wouldn’t write this today, but rework the sentence to be plural or even use the "singular they." We would not default to the male term. So why on earth would we think it’s ok to use some sort of "inclusive male term" for two women grads of SNL? I found it very sexist.

With apologies, I won't be entering the fray of ALUMNI vs ALUMNAE;
I'm too busy committing Naoero to memory now that Nauru has officially changed its name. 
Look at all those vowels! I'm banking on it showing up in a crossword in the future...

As for today's shout-out to an Indian wedding, it was cute wordplay, but I got more enjoyment out of the rest of the fill because I'm usually not a good audience for dad jokes. It's a rare one that makes me laugh, not groan, and that's on me.

It's a wonder Nabisco hasn't put out a limited edition of packages that come with a collector's edition booklet of all the OREO clues ever published in the NYT crosswords.

That said this was a decent grid for a Tuesday, and I enjoyed it on that basis alone (although count me as one who agrees that ALUMNI is a clear unforced error and ACER is clunky).

Have to ask though, if you were trying to impress by going out with a great civil rights leader, would that be ARMGANDHI? (He was a DAL, wasn’t he?). I almost had another less well known politician as my date, but luckily avoided that—it was a NEHRU escape.)

If you ignore that just to make some point or try to change the language unilaterally, how is that any different than saying they are two MEN just because you feel Ike it? I don’t get it.

Without dipping my toe too deeply into the swamp, may I say that: for Amy Pohler and Tina Fey, two graduates, who happen to be women, of an institution which include both men and women in equal numbers, it is better to use "alumni"; whereas for graduates of a (traditionally) all-women institution, such as Radcliffe or Vassar, it is better to use "alumnæ." (and, people, don't forget the ligature!) Several days ago, someone--@Lucky13?--mentioned the seminal* book *Language and Women's Place*, by the feminist linguist Robin Lakoff (who identified as a cis-woman, I believe). In it, Ms. Lakoff argues that more would be accomplished by striving to erase inequalities in connotation, such as "adventurer vs. adventuress" that to redefine grammar (alumna/-us, she vs. they). (LaWP was published in 1975; I wonder if Ms. Lakoff's views changed since then?) https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=garNxavx8gY&t=1s (Look, Sam--a whole battery of mice!) *"seminal"--what a patriarchal word!

On a related but separate topic, I’ve been thinking how odd it is that we still have separate categories for Best Actress in Emmys, Oscars, etc. There’s none for best female director, etc. I’m assuming that when they were first instituted, there was an assumption that 1) chauvinistically men were intrinsically better actors (I hope not) 2) women’s acting “style” was just different and couldn’t be compared fairly or 3) women didn’t have access to the same quality or type of roles. It seems likely only 3) would still potentially be the case, but at least not to the same degree, I hope. 

Still I wonder why today, given the additional wrinkle of gender preference/identification (both for actors and roles) why we don’t just, say, make one acting award (or give two to the top two actors if we still want an extra award). It just seems a bit anachronistic. This is not the same, after all, as separate sports for men and women, which is a can of worms I don’t want to open and in any case doesn’t apply. If you think that women are still hampered professionally as actors, and deserve a separate award for that reason, that’s a legitimate argument, although we should then be striving for more equity and a day when there doesn’t need to be two separate awards. What do you all think?

In the alumni/alumnae debate, some people have accused the constructor/editor of "misgendering" Tina Fey and Amy Poehler.

Is this the right approach? Are we better off as a society if we get upset and accuse people of ill intent? Or is it better to acknowledge that this could be an honest mistake and move on?

If the Mario puzzle taught us anything, it's that sometimes we can become so caught up in our "sphere of influence" that we assume our experiences are universal.

So are we doing society better by giving each other grace, or is it better to react with anger -- realizing that we push people away from our side by putting people on the defensive, but believing that this will ultimately be more likely to produce change? It's an interesting question.

Re ALUMNI, there seem to be multiple issues here. First, was the ALUMNI clue off or suboptimal? I think that one's obvious. In last night's first comment, I said as much. Second, can the clue be justified nonetheless? Here I think there might be enough wiggle room, surprising as it might be. This Merriam-Webster usage note states (note especially the last sentence): "For the plurals, alumni refers to multiple male or gender neutral graduates, alumnae is for multiple female grads, and alums is the gender neutral plural. These terms are often used loosely and their strict definitions are in flux." And also: "Alumni = plural male graduates & plural gender neutral graduates" And: "When used in a more figurative sense (“a person who is a former member, employee, contributor, or inmate”) alumnus and alumni tend to be less gendered." https://www.merriam-webster.com/grammar/alumni-or-alumnus-usage-guide I know what your English teacher taught you, and I know how many of you feel about it, myself included, but I think this one might just squeak by. Third, did Will Shortz and crew make a mistake? I don't think they're that clueless, so to speak. They've found that ALUMNI is now being used more broadly; they're allowing common usage to prevail. On purpose. In baseball, it's a strike if just the edge of the ball grazes the strike zone; the new challenge system makes that clear. I think this one is much like that pitch that looks inside but just clips the edge of the zone.

Mrs. Lakoff was married to George Lakoff. He was a student of Noam Chomsky. They studied transformational grammar and other areas of linguistics. These studies were the basis of teaching computers to talk, as I understand it.

Transformational grammar looks at the "surface structure" versus the "deep structure" of language. In other words: what is the subject of the sentence "Skiing is fun"? Traditionally, people would say "skiing" is the subject. But transformational grammarians will say the subject is "I" because the "deep structure" of the sentence is "I like skiing."

That's how commputers learn to talk.

1) strictly speaking a Natick is when two potentially obscure entries (usually proper nouns) cross and the crossing letter is not obvious phonetically, so at best you have to guess. It is called a Natick because that is a small town in Massachusetts that potentially only locals would know, so if it crosses something else obscure you might not know what letter to enter.

With all due respect to D and his right to his own opinion, I don’t think his examples are the best because, say, IPOS and NYSE are such common fodder for crosswords that most of us know them from that; but there’s a case to be made for “personal” Naticks and if D is not aware of those terms then it’s true there is no way he could guess them. And for AC_R and T_RI you could argue that the missing letter ought to be guessable from context or common phonetics, but again YMMV, not trying to disrespect D, just clarify the concept.

2) the “uproar”, such as it is, is that we deal with words here and if we can’t use them correctly in a crossword clue, then where can we? That’s a different argument than less common usage of words, variants, deliberate misdirection, changes in language usage, etc. which I fully support and embrace. It’s just that no one has given me enough evidence that that applies here.

I am from MA and am very familiar with the city of Natick (shout out to Cuffy, may he rest in peace).
